method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Consider whether anxiety contributes to every child's presentation.** **Psychological therapy is first-line and ongoing**; any medication goes alongside it.
claims.source_text: Consider whether anxiety is contributing to the presentation for all children Psychological therapy should be first line and ongoing treatment for anxiety If medication is being considered, this should be in conjunction with ongoing psychological therapy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Anxiety disorders differ from normal anxiety by intensity, duration and impact on daily function.**
claims.source_text: While some degree of anxiety is recognised as a normal response to stress, anxiety disorders can be distinguished by their intensity, duration and impact on daily function
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for:** regular avoidance (school, social events, play, sport, eating, sleeping) · frequent tummy aches and headaches · outbursts or meltdowns · poor sleep · appetite change · frequent reassurance-seeking · poor concentration · overplanning and overthinking.
claims.source_text: Regularly avoiding everyday experiences and situations, eg school, social events, playing, sport, eating or sleeping Frequent physical complaints, such as tummy aches and headaches Sudden emotional or angry outbursts, tantrums or 'meltdowns' Difficulty sleeping Changes in appetite Seeking reassurance often Being preoccupied or unable to concentrate Overplanning situations and overthinking things
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check against DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria**; screening tools (Spence, SCARED, Social phobia inventory) help but **must be supplemented by clinical interview and observation.**
claims.source_text: Assess for symptoms of anxiety disorder and determine whether symptoms meet diagnostic criteria in DSM-5 or ICD-11 … Rating scales and screening tools may be useful in assessing anxiety but must be supplemented by clinical interview and observations when making a diagnosis. A variety of screening instruments are available including Spence children's anxiety scale SCARED Social phobia inventory
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors include** neurodevelopmental disorders (autism, ADHD, intellectual disability), other mental health conditions, chronic illness, sensory impairment, gender-related concerns, trauma, family history of anxiety, depression, OCD or substance use, and substance misuse.
claims.source_text: Neurodevelopmental disorders eg autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual disability … Mental health conditions eg eating disorders … Chronic illness that impacts daily functioning, quality of life, autonomy eg cystic fibrosis Sensory impairment Gender-related concerns Experience of trauma … Family history of anxiety, depression, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) or substance use disorders Substance misuse
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine:** baseline cardiac exam, BP, heart rate and growth; targeted exam to rule out mimics such as **hyperthyroidism**. **No investigations** unless considering an alternative diagnosis.
claims.source_text: Baseline physical exam including cardiac exam, blood pressure, heart rate and growth parameters Further targeted exam as indicated, to rule out organic causes that may mimic anxiety symptoms eg hyperthyroidism … No investigations are required unless considering an alternative diagnosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Always start with psychoeducation**, then the psychological and medication options acceptable to child and family.
claims.source_text: A discussion of treatment and support options should always begin with psychoeducation, followed by consideration of the psychological and medication treatment options acceptable to the child and family
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CBT is first line for ages 8–18 with mild–moderate symptoms**, before considering medication. **Internet CBT** (eg BRAVE, Cool Kids) suits children 8 and over.
claims.source_text: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) should be used for remission of anxiety diagnosis, reduction of anxiety symptoms and improvement in daily functioning of children aged 8-18, who have mild-moderate symptoms, as a first line treatment before considering medication … Evidence informed Internet CBT (CBT using online/app-based programs) can be used for children ≥8 yo with anxiety, individually or with assistance, depending on age/developmental stage BRAVE Program Cool Kids Anxiety Program
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Play therapy** for under-8s, procedural anxiety or medical trauma, or under-12s who struggle with CBT; **ACT** for 12–18-year-olds, especially with chronic health conditions.
claims.source_text: Play therapy could be considered for children <8 yo, those with procedural anxiety or medical trauma, or those <12 yo who have may have difficulty engaging in CBT Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) could be used for children and young people 12-18 yo, particularly for those with concurrent chronic health conditions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Medication is not first line except in exceptional circumstances**, and is best started by a clinician experienced in paediatric psychotropic prescribing.
claims.source_text: Should not be considered a first-line treatment except in exceptional circumstances Best initiated by a clinician with knowledge, training, and experience in prescribing psychotropic medications in children
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Add medication to therapy if anxiety is** too severe for meaningful therapy · significantly limiting school attendance · carrying moderate or greater self-harm risk · a significant risk to a family member's wellbeing. **Continue therapy alongside.**
claims.source_text: Could be used in conjunction with psychological therapies if the child's anxiety is: Too severe to allow meaningful engagement in psychological therapy and medication may assist associated with significantly reduced access to education due to limited school attendance associated with a moderate or greater risk of deliberate self-harm* associated with a significant risk to the wellbeing of the family member Psychological therapy should be continued in conjunction with medication
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Starting medication may not reduce self-harm risk and may increase agitation at first** (activation syndrome).
claims.source_text: associated with a moderate or greater risk of deliberate self-harm* … *NB commencing medications may not reduce this risk and may increase agitation initially. See side effects/activation syndrome below
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **SSRIs are first-line medication**, prescribed **off label** — none is TGA-licensed for anxiety or depression in children. **Fluoxetine and escitalopram are sensible choices** (FDA-approved for depressive episodes).
claims.source_text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line medication for anxiety As no SSRIs are currently licensed by TGA for use in anxiety or depression in children and adolescents in Australia, medications will be prescribed off label … As fluoxetine and escitalopram are approved by FDA for depressive episodes, it is sensible to consider using these
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Example doses — fluoxetine** (tab, liquid): start 5–10 mg, change by 5–10 mg, typical 20–40 mg.
claims.source_text: An example of common prescribing patterns below SSRI Forms Starting dose +/- by Typical dose Fluoxetine Tab, liquid 5-10 mg 5-10 mg 20-40 mg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sertraline** (tab): start 12.5–25 mg, change by 12.5–25 mg, typical 50–100 mg.
claims.source_text: Sertraline Tab 12.5-25 mg 12.5-25 mg 50-100 mg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Escitalopram** (tab): start 5 mg, change by 5 mg, typical 10–20 mg.
claims.source_text: Escitalopram Tab 5 mg 5 mg 10-20 mg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start low and titrate slowly** to the minimum effective dose; **effect takes several weeks** and keeps building over months. Unfamiliar prescribers should discuss with a senior clinician.
claims.source_text: When commencing medication, start with a low dose, noting that doses vary depending on age, developmental stage and symptoms … Those unfamiliar with prescribing SSRIs should discuss with senior clinician titrate up slowly whilst monitoring for adverse effects to reach a minimum effective dose SSRIs take several weeks to become effective for anxiety and the benefits, when seen, often continue to increase over time (months)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Activation syndrome** — more activity, impulsivity, disinhibition, restlessness, irritability, insomnia. **Use caution, low doses and slow up-titration** in highly aroused/ADHD children, family history of bipolar disorder, and younger children.
claims.source_text: Activation syndrome is a well-known adverse effect of SSRIs and presents with increased activity, impulsivity, disinhibition, restlessness, irritability, and insomnia Caution when prescribing SSRIs is recommended for the following children: highly aroused/ADHD with comorbid anxiety family history of bipolar disorder younger age Dosing needs to be low, and up-titration should be done slowly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Common adverse effects:** nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, dry mouth, agitation, insomnia or sedation, headache, dizziness, sweating, sexual dysfunction. **Taper SSRIs gradually**; prefer a long half-life such as fluoxetine if adherence is a concern.
claims.source_text: Most common - nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dry mouth, agitation, insomnia (or sometimes sedation), headaches, dizziness, sweating and sexual dysfunction SSRIs should be gradually reduced to minimise discontinuation symptoms Consider SSRIs with longer half-lives eg fluoxetine, or those deemed to be at lower risk of discontinuation syndrome if concern about medication adherence
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adjust:** partial effect — consider increasing; intolerable side effects — reduce or stop; **ineffective at tolerated doses after a reasonable trial (eg 8 weeks) — stop and change**, first to another SSRI.
claims.source_text: Some, but limited effectiveness of medication Consider a dose increase Side effects that are not tolerated Consider dose decrease or medication cessation Tolerated therapeutic doses ineffective after reasonable trial (eg 8 weeks) Consider medication cessation and change … When considering medication changes for a child who has been taking SSRIs, the first change to consider is to another SSRI
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Short-acting benzodiazepines may be cautiously considered for an acute crisis in high-risk settings** (eg ED).
claims.source_text: Clinicians could cautiously consider the use of short acting benzodiazepines to assist in the management of an acute crisis in high-risk settings (eg emergency department)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Not recommended for anxiety disorders alone:** antipsychotics, clonidine, guanfacine, atomoxetine, reboxetine, tricyclic antidepressants.
claims.source_text: Anti-psychotic medications, alpha-2 agonists (clonidine and guanfacine), atomoxetine, reboxetine and tricyclic antidepressants are not recommended for the treatment of anxiety disorders in isolation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use rating scales (eg RCADS) throughout; on starting medication, review response and adverse effects every 2 weeks** until stable.
claims.source_text: Symptom and adverse effect rating scales (eg RCADS) should be used throughout the course of both psychological and medication treatment … On medication initiation, and while establishing stability, clinical response and adverse effects should be reviewed every 2 weeks
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Involve Child and Adolescent Mental Health** if anxiety is complicated by other mental health problems, carries significant risk to the child or others, or is beyond the clinician's comfort.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local Child and Adolescent Mental Health specialist when Anxiety presentation with any of the following complicated by coexisting mental health problems significant risk identified for patient or others beyond the comfort of the clinician
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Discharge only after a risk assessment for harm to self or others deems it safe**, with follow-up arranged — usually ongoing.
claims.source_text: Risk assessment regarding risk of harm to self or others completed and deemed safe for discharge Appropriate follow up arranged. Children with anxiety will likely require ongoing follow up with a paediatrician or other appropriate clinician
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anxiety: identification and management' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anxiety__identification_and_management/, retrieved 2026-09-23
